5|Clinical Measures
6|The primary outcome was average pain over the last week on
7|a numerical rating scale from 0 to 10 from the Brief Pain
8|Inventory Short Form, assessed at the 1-month postbaseline
9|session. We also calculated the proportion of participants re-
10|porting pain reduction of 30% or more, pain reduction of 50%
11|or more, and a pain score of 0 or 1, indicating a pain-free or
12|nearly pain-free state. Secondary outcomes included pain in-
13|terference (Oswestry Disability Index); Patient-Reported Out-
14|come Measurement Information System (PROMIS) short forms
15|for depression, anxiety, anger, and sleep quality; and the Posi-
16|tiveandNegativeAffectScale(measuredetailsintheeMethods
17|in Supplement 2).
18|We considered 3 measures of pain beliefs as potential me-
19|diators: (1) the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11), assess-
20|ing belief that pain indicates injury and fear of movement;
21|(2) the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS); and (3) the Survey
22|of Pain Attitudes Emotion subscale (SOPA-Emotion), assess-
23|ing beliefs that stress and negative emotion increase pain. Ad-
24|verse events were recorded when participants spontane-
25|ously reported them to study personnel. Baseline pain was
26|computed as the average score from 2 prerandomization
27|assessments (eligibility session and pretreatment fMRI
28|session).
29|Neuroimaging Measures
30|Structural T1 and multiband blood oxygenation level-
31|dependent functional imaging was conducted on a 3-T
32|Siemens Prisma Fit MRI scanner with standard fMRI prepro-
33|cessing (eMethods in Supplement 2). During fMRI, partici-
34|pants completed (1) an evoked back pain task with a series of
35|randomly ordered trials distending the back to 1 of 4 intensity
36|levels and (2) a spontaneous pain scan in which participants
37|rested and rated ongoing pain once per minute (design de-
38|tails in the eMethods in Supplement 2; fMRI data quality mea-
39|sures shown in eFigures 6 and 7 in Supplement 2). Partici-
40|pants rated pain during scanning on a visual analog scale from
41|0 (no pain) to 100 (worst pain imaginable).
42|Statistical Analyses
43|Intent-to-treat analyses (including all randomized patients)
44|were performed for the primary outcome with a mixed-
45|effects model (fitlme, MATLAB 2020a), including 2 group ×
46|time interactions (PRT vs placebo × posttreatment vs pretreat-
47|ment and PRT vs usual care × posttreatment vs pretreat-
48|ment), covariates for age and sex, and a random intercept per
49|participant. Treatment response rates for 30% or greater re-
50|duction in pain, 50% or greater reduction in pain, and a pain-
51|free or nearly pain-free state at posttreatment and 1-year fol-
52|low-up were based on all randomized patients; those missing
53|datawereconsiderednonresponders.Forfollow-uptimepoints
54|and secondary outcomes, we calculated Hedges g for the PRT
55|vs placebo and PRT vs usual care comparisons. Follow-up time
56|points were analyzed individually, testing group differences
57|in change from baseline to each time points. The placebo vs
58|usual care comparison will be reported elsewhere.

12|Clinical Outcomes
13|Patients randomized to PRT reported substantial reductions
14|in pain intensity at posttreatment compared with both con-
15|trol groups, with a mean (SD) pain score of 1.18 (1.24) in the
16|PRT group, 2.84 (1.64) in the placebo group, and 3.13 (1.45) in
17|the usual care group (Figure 2; Table 2). Patients in the PRT
18|group reported a pain reduction of 1.79 (on the 0 to 10
19|numerical rating scale) relative to placebo (t137.63 = 6.06;
20|P < .001; g, -1.14; 95% CI, -1.65 to -0.71) and reported a
21|pain reduction of 2.40 relative to the usual care group
22|(t135.69 = 8.13; P < .001; g, -1.74; 95% CI, -2.28 to -1.32).
